II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01230

(Perhaps this was one of the reasons why Avicennism eventually disappeared from the medieval West.) This prophetic philosophy is also “speculative” in the original sense of the word, which is connected with the idea of a mirror. As our anonymous Sufi explains, whenever the prophet needs knowledge, he turns the mirror of his soul (âyîna-ye jân, speculum animae) toward the “holy world” to receive from it the true Reality (haqîqat).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01231

Just as a figure becomes present in a mirror through reflection, taking on the particular coloring of that mirror, so these true Realities become actual within the prophet. They are the truths of spiritual knowledge projected into him from the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh mahfûz)—that is, from the heavenly fullness of sacred essences that have not yet appeared in the visible world. The image of the mirror constantly recurs in the writings of these spiritual thinkers. The interpenetration of spirit and body leads them to conceive of a spiritual embodiment and a bodily spirituality (compare the Geistleiblichkeit found in Oetinger, Schelling, and others).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01232

But for them this interpenetration cannot mean what Christian dogma calls the Incarnation, because the Incarnation involves a self-emptying (kenosis) of the divine into flesh. Here, by contrast, the interpenetration of spirit and body can produce only a transfiguration, an elevation of the bodily into a higher mode of being. The result is an intermediate world with an existence of its own, situated between the spiritual and bodily worlds: the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world (’âlam al-mithâl), “where spirits take on bodies and bodies become spiritual.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01233

As we know, visionary mystics can enter this world in dreams or ecstasy, or even while awake—though in the waking state it requires a distinctive mystical way of perceiving reality. Such perception transforms reality, giving it the radiance and depth of a mirror through which something else shines. The mystic perceives the world as the “form of manifestation” (mazhar) of an invisible spiritual reality.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01234

Yet that invisible reality is not incorporated into the substance of the sensible world. It is not present there as an accidental quality inhering in a substance. Rather, it is present precisely as an image is present in a mirror—and that is why it becomes visible. The word “Docetism” is generally invoked to ridicule the gnostics who professed it, as though they had been content with mere phantoms. In reality, when the sensible world becomes the bearer of a divine manifestation, when it is raised to the condition of a mirror, it may indeed lose the privileged solidity that ordinary outward perception attributes to it. Such perception may judge that, once made transparent, the world has become nothing but appearance.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01235

But in truth it has become not merely an appearance, but nothing less than the place where a spiritual reality appears (mazhar). Only in this way can we understand the role of the letter and its literal meaning in the transcendent interpretation practiced by Sufism and Ismailism. When our author, following his predecessors, says that the prophet's soul functions as a mirror, we must keep these considerations in mind.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01236

The invisible appears within this mirror according to the mirror's capacity to make it manifest, and it takes on the mirror's coloring—just as water takes on the color of the glass containing it. The prophet's soul is here the subjectum incarnationis, the subject or bearer of incarnation, if it is not too paradoxical to speak of a “spiritual incarnation.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01237

But the event is not complete until the complementary process takes place. Once the spiritual has taken bodily form through the prophet's soul, the bodily must itself be spiritualized through the work of the interpreter—who, in Shiite terms, is the Imam. According to our treatise, what is given to the prophet's “holy intellect” in an immaterial and universal form is reflected and multiplied within it. It assumes a “real appearance” by clothing itself in sounds and letters, so that the prophet's message becomes understandable to the community to which he has been sent. It is because of this process—the “embodiment of the spiritual” in the mirror of the prophet's soul—that the outward meaning of the Qur'an (zâhir) is the meaning (ma’nâ) we gather from its letters and sounds, from the words composed of them.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01238

The inward meaning (bâtin), the hidden depth of the Qur'an, is the true Reality itself: the divine Word that subsists eternally with and through the divine Selfhood, and manifests itself in the body of letters and literal meaning just as an image appears in a mirror. To reach this true Reality of the Qur'an, to gain spiritual knowledge of the divine Word, the interpreter must therefore accomplish the complementary operation, reversing the first: the spiritualization of the bodily.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01239

Otherwise the event of divine manifestation would remain unfinished, and its purity would be endangered. It would fall into one of two traps: holûl, the idea of incarnation or indwelling, or enslavement to the literal text. These are two aspects of the same materialization, the same complete darkening of the mirror. Interpreting the inward meaning must bring about a kind of “dematerialization”: the restoration of matter and the letter to their essential, spiritual state.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01240

Only this operation makes it possible to “perceive the fragrance of the other world.” And if the operation proceeds through seven depths, seven inward meanings, that is because there are correspondingly seven levels of spiritual seekers. Their hierarchy reflects the seven stages of ascent (’orûj), through which the matter of the Book's letters and sounds is raised to its essential reality. This ascent is the great work of ta’wîl: interpreting the Book by leading it back to its spiritual meaning, its original inward reality.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01241

The work of ta’wîl is conceived as an ascent that is, at the same time, a descent into the depths. That is why the Prophet's ecstatic ascent on the night of the Mi’râj becomes the model of the highest mystical experience: an ascent into the ultimate depth. Our author can now deal briefly with ordinary outward exegesis, the kind that restricts itself to literal meaning.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01242
“This is a form of knowledge,” he says, “through which one must pass. It is the starting point, the entrance, the threshold. But one must cross that threshold and enter the interior.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01243

This knowledge is drawn from the traditional Qur'anic sciences as a whole: lexicography, grammar, syntax, the rules of recitation, the study of verses that abrogate other verses and those that have been abrogated, the study of narratives, and so forth.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01244
“But all these sciences, when compared with the true Realities and the spiritual knowledge contained in the Qur'an, are merely empty husks, skins, and discarded coverings.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01245

“However distinguished the commentators on the literal meaning may be—the outward interpreters (mofassirân-e zâhir) and the authorities of religious law—and however elevated their pronouncements may sound, all of it, everything they teach, is still no more than a husk, an empty shell. Perhaps only one person in a thousand possesses knowledge of the hidden spiritual meaning. Even among a great multitude, the number who possess it is very small. Most people know and understand nothing of the Qur'an beyond the letters written on paper.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01246
Our author then quotes a Persian couplet:
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01247
“No wonder that their share of the Qur'an is nothing more than the letter. The eye of a blind man, facing the sun, feels only its warmth—not its light.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
en-book-4-ch-2-s3
3. The Seven Inner Depths and the Hierarchy of Spiritual Seekers
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01248

“As for the seven depths or inward meanings of the Qur'an,” our author continues, “they designate a succession of hidden meanings understood respectively by seven groups of people. Each group understands according to its own capacity, its degree of preparation, and the subtlety of its contemplation.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01249

We know that every initiatory experience can be described either as a descent or as an ascent. It is simultaneously a movement toward the center of the Sphere and toward the celestial pole. This is why a descent into the depths of inward meaning corresponds to the Prophet's ascent from Heaven to Heaven. Equally, as our author is careful to point out, each new level of depth can be described as a higher level of elevation.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01250

A simple diagram of the system of concentric celestial spheres would be enough to make this language visually intelligible. To characterize each of the Qur'an's seven depths, the author takes a particular description of the Book from the Qur'anic text itself. Each description becomes the key that determines the distinctive character of that level.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01251

1) The first depth: the pious ascetics At the first depth, the character of the Qur'anic text is established by the description of it as the “Book that brings the Reminder” (wa’l-Qorâni dhî’l-dhikr, 38:1), the Book that is the great Reminder. This first inward meaning, the first stage in the spiritual landscape, corresponds to the inner life and religion of the “mystical wayfarer” (sâlik). Having responded to the Reminder, the wayfarer has set foot upon the Path in order to acquire the first elements of spiritual formation. These consist above all of the various forms of spiritual struggle (mojâhada).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01252

Indeed, Sufism has sometimes understood itself as consisting essentially in this kind of discipline, as happened in early Mesopotamian Sufism during the first centuries of the Islamic era. At this initial level, then, the Qur'an—whose literal appearance presents it as the code of a religious Law—reveals itself as a guide to the individual's inner life. It is read and meditated upon as a practical handbook of spiritual struggle.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01253

Interpretation discovers throughout the details of the text allusions to the states and trials through which entry onto the mystical path becomes possible: firm resolve, willing acceptance, trusting surrender, patience, inner tranquility, and so on. The people who put into practice this first inward meaning, corresponding to their spiritual capacity, are called the “pious ascetics” (ahl-e riyâza). 2) The second depth: the Sufis At the second depth, the character of the Qur'an is established by its designation as the “Noble Book” (Qorân karîm, 56:76). This second inward level expresses the way of being and spiritual dwelling place of the Sufis (ahl-e tasavvof).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01254

Through their understanding of this meaning, they move beyond the mere asceticism of the preceding group and enter the states of spiritual experience: the stations (maqâmât), degrees (madârij), and successive stages (ma’ârij) familiar to those who practice Sufism. They learn to understand everything implied by the term mokâshafa, inward revelation or intuitive unveiling. They learn to distinguish the meaning of the moment (waqt), the passing spiritual state (hâl), ecstasy (wajd), mystical perception or taste (dhawq), mystical intoxication (sokr), wakefulness, the soul's contraction or anguish (qabz), expansion (bast), and so forth. They then interpret the whole Qur'an using the technical language of Sufism, because this second inward meaning reveals the Qur'an to them as a guide to the psychology of mystical experience. It is possible that our author had in mind mystical commentaries such as those of Sulami and Qushayri.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01255

3) The third depth: the philosophers Descending one degree further, we reach a level of interpretation characterized by the description of the Qur'an as the “Wise Book” (Qorân hakîm, 36:1). This is the inward meaning that reveals itself to philosophers (ahl-e hikmat), shapes their inner being, and determines their spiritual place. By penetrating the meaning that belongs specifically to their level, they perceive the objects of philosophical knowledge (ma’qûlât) concealed beneath the literal appearance.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01256

To write a Qur'anic commentary from this perspective is to show how the sacred text, beneath the veil of its allusions, answers to the demands of philosophical knowledge. Such matters include the affirmation of the First Principle (Mabda’ avval), the emanation of multiplicity from that First Principle through a hierarchy of intermediate hypostases, and related questions. We may think here of Avicenna's commentaries on certain surahs, his Epistle on the Angels, and other works. 4) The fourth depth: the gnostics and theosophers
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01257

At a higher—or deeper—level than that of the philosopher in the ordinary sense stands the spiritual seeker designated by the term ’ârif, usually translated as “gnostic.” This translation is technically accurate. It indicates a kinship with the kind of knowledge common to the various traditions of gnosis, without implying anything beyond that. More precisely, the distinction between philosopher and gnostic (hakîm and ’ârif) corresponds here to the distinction established by Suhrawardi, the master of Illumination (Ishrâq).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01258

The preceding group consisted of philosophers in whom mystical experience was not yet assumed to be present. The present group consists of the theosophers (hakîm ilâhî), who unite philosophical knowledge with mystical experience. The Qur'an as these seekers read and understand it—the Qur'an whose meaning takes shape within them spiritually—is characterized by the designation “Luminous Book” or “Translucent Book” (Qorân mobîn, 15:1). By penetrating the inward meaning corresponding to their way of being, they perceive the divine secrets (asrâr-e ilâhî) and the higher teachings of spiritual knowledge (ma’ârif-e haqîqî) concealed within the text's outward appearance.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01259

We may think here of certain monumental works still entirely unknown in the West: the mystical commentaries of Ibn Arabi and his disciples, Semnani, and Haydar Amoli; and the commentary later produced in seventeenth-century Iran by Mulla Sadra Shirazi, a student of Mir Damad, the great master of Illuminationist theosophy in the Safavid period. There would, admittedly, be just as much reason to associate these commentaries with the seventh inward level described below. Faced with works of such immense scale and doctrinal depth, one senses the presence of an extraordinary spiritual adventure, for which the Qur'an serves as both nourishment and guide.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01260

Until we undertake their comparative study, the fundamental problems of interpretation raised throughout this work, as well as research into the nature of mystical experience more generally, will remain deprived of evidence of extraordinary importance and impressive scope. 5) The fifth depth: the faithful of love The fifth inward meaning is characterized by the description of the Qur'an as the “Glorious Book” (Qorân majîd, 85:21). The reference to the “Preserved Tablet” (85:22), upon which the Book has been inscribed since the very beginning, also directs us toward the heavenly archetype of that Book.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01261

The spiritual group corresponding to this degree of inward understanding is that of the “mystical lovers” (’oshshâq). More precisely, they are those whom we have already called the “faithful of love,” because of their affinity with those in the West who, in the circle surrounding Dante, gave themselves that name: the Fedeli d'amore. It is important to notice that, according to our author, this name is by no means interchangeable with the simple designation “Sufis.” He placed the devout Sufis in general at the first two levels.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01262

The faithful of love stand much higher: at the fifth degree of spiritual elevation or inward depth. In fact, Sufism had to struggle to gain acceptance for the term ’ishq—eros, passionate love—as a description of the believer's relationship with God. The very conception of divinity was at stake. To conceive and experience this divine eros, a person must open himself to an undivided, personal manifestation of God. The result is a mysticism of bridal love, toward which the communal and egalitarian religious consciousness of monotheism understood primarily as Law could feel only alarm and jealousy.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01263

Hallaj, Suhrawardi, Attar, Ruzbihan, Jalal Rumi, Ibn Arabi, and so many others, together with all their disciples, were the heroes of this religion of love. They lived and read the Qur'an as though it were a version of the Song of Songs. Their interpretation discovers in every passage of the Book a sign of the Beloved. It comments upon the text by transforming all its words into symbols of love. Our author knows that the faithful of love do not shrink from any of the daring expressions technically known as shathîyât.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01264

As we have explained (Book III above), this term corresponds etymologically to the Greek paradoxa: paradoxes, astonishing and incredible declarations, statements that overturn all received ideas. The Arabic root shth evokes the idea of falling backward in astonishment. For the rigidly orthodox believer, such paradoxical declarations are nothing but scandalous blasphemies and acts of unbelief. For the passionate mystic, who may declare, for example, “Without me, God could not exist for a single instant,” they are, at most, “pious blasphemies” or “beautiful acts of unbelief.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01265

Earlier (Book III), we mentioned the great work in which Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz collected and interpreted a large number of these paradoxical sayings—a major monument of Sufism. It is possible that our anonymous author was thinking of Ruzbihan here. 6) The sixth depth: those who realize divine Unity At the sixth depth, the distinctive character is established by the description of the Qur'an as the “Venerable Book” (Qorân ’azîz, 41:41).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01266

Our author is rather reserved about identifying the spiritual group to which this level, and the following one, correspond. He describes this sixth group as those who have realized within themselves and through their own being the inward meaning of tawhîd, the affirmation of divine Unity. They are the Mowahhidân, whom we may call the “unifiers”: those who have experienced fanâ’ in its true sense. What they experience is the hidden absorption into divinity of everything that ordinary, naive, or merely literal knowledge imagines and treats as existence outside God. The path of these unifiers is marked by successive stations (maqâmât) in the inward realization of tawhîd. Its culmination is not the destruction or annihilation of the mystic as a person.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01267

Rather, it is a fanâ’ that abolishes the opacity of a being who formerly existed only “for himself,” because his ego absorbed the whole of the being entrusted to him. The mode of heightened existence (baqâ’) that follows fanâ’ then gives him the transparency of a mirror. He acquires the capacity to become a place of divine manifestation (mazhar). 7) The seventh depth: the one who has arrived We are now prepared for the inward realization corresponding to the seventh meaning, characterized by the description of the Qur'an as the “Sublime Book” (Qorân ’azîm, 15:87).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01268

Here lies the goal of every station along the mystical Path. It is the spiritual dwelling place of “the one who has arrived” (wâsil), the person who has attained union. His entire being gathers together the different ways in which the divine Attributes become manifest. He has become the mirror in which the radiance of pre-eternal Subsistence is reflected. And because he contemplates the divine manifestations (tajallî) in the mirror that he himself has become, he is truly their eyewitness. This seems to be the level at which the saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” has been realized so completely that its truth also makes the reverse true:
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01269
“Through knowing his Lord, he comes to know himself.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01270
For after fanâ’, the soul perceives itself at once as uncreated and as a creature. At this point, another saying becomes especially significant. Our author associates it with this mystical station:
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01271
“Whoever has seen me has seen God” (man ra’ânî faqad ra’a al-Haqq).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01272

This declaration, which seems to be a transposition of a passage from the Gospel of John (14:7 and 19), was especially cherished and meditated upon in Shiite circles. It expresses the Shiite understanding of divine manifestation as something accomplished in the heavenly person of the Imam. The Imam is the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal Human Being, in whose person the invisible and unknowable God becomes visible to the eye of the heart. At the deepest level of inward interpretation, therefore, the operation we previously described as the necessary complement to the first is accomplished.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01273

Following the example of the Prophet, the mystic's soul becomes a pure mirror. And what appears within that mirror is the heavenly Anthropos, the eternal Imam. The relationship is the same as that between the prophet who proclaims (Nâtiq) and the silent Imam (Sâmit). It is also the same as that between the letter of the sacred Book, transformed into a symbol, and the spiritual meaning that becomes manifest through it. Here we reach the final goal of both prophetic philosophy and the interpretation of inward meaning.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01274

On the divine side, there is the taking of human form at the level of the Imam's heavenly humanity—the figure who, in Ismailism, bears the name Melchizedek. Corresponding to this, on the human side, is the taking on of divine form (ta’alloh, theôsis): the transformation of the human being through mystical experience. Here we should recall everything Haydar Amoli observed concerning the relationship between Shiism and Sufism.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01275

Later we shall try to analyze the implications of Semnani's interpretive method. His extraordinary tafsîr, embracing all seven hidden meanings, properly belongs at this seventh inward level. Admittedly, the other Qur'anic commentaries mentioned earlier, in our discussion of the fourth level, could equally well be placed here. That a thinker who is explicitly Shiite should find the understanding of the Imam at the very end and summit of mystical experience is something another previously unpublished Persian treatise will now show us. We owe this next work to an eminent Iranian Shiite philosopher and mystic of the fifteenth century.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01276
Chapter III A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s1
1. The Inner Meaning of the Splitting of the Moon
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01277

Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî belonged to a Shiite family originally from Turkestan that later settled in Isfahan. During the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries (the eighth and ninth centuries of the Hijra), the family produced a distinguished succession of scholars.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01278

Sa’inoddin, who died in Herat in 830/1427, gives us an exceptionally revealing picture of the learning and intellectual interests of a mystical philosopher in Iran at that time. He was thoroughly familiar with Suhrawardî’s philosophy of Light (Ishrâq) and understood its deeper meaning. He wrote commentaries on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs and on the great Persian mystical poem by Mahmûd Shabestarî. He was a Shiite whose philosophical and mystical thinking drew nourishment from works of this kind. His own writings thus helped shape a specifically Shiite theosophy, close in spirit to the original inspiration from which Ismaili gnosis had itself emerged.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01279

In Iran, meanwhile, following the fall of Alamût in 1257, Ismailism had reorganized itself while retreating, to varying degrees, into secrecy. Its influence was all the more active for being less visible. It can be felt throughout later Iranian Sufism and is especially apparent in the emergence, during the fourteenth century, of the school known as Hurufism. Its followers cultivated a mystical science of letters whose tradition reaches back to the beginnings of Shiism. Within Islam, they are the closest counterparts to the Kabbalists. Sa’inoddin himself was a Shiite hurufi, a practitioner of this letter mysticism, and that fact left a deep mark on his thought.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01280

Among his writings is a short Persian treatise particularly well suited to helping us understand how meaning becomes inwardly realized. The anonymous author discussed in the preceding chapter showed us that this process of inward understanding determines the hierarchy and spiritual character of different kinds of seekers. Sa’inoddin’s treatise offers something like a practical exercise in the interpretation of a Quranic verse, designed to test the hierarchy of different forms of consciousness through the ways they understand it. His chosen text is the first verse of surah 54, the Surah of the Moon: The Hour drew near, and the Moon split apart.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01281
Hence the title of his treatise: The Treatise on the Splitting of the Moon.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01282

Interpreters who insist on the literal meaning of the Quran have had considerable difficulty giving this verse a coherent explanation, particularly in establishing a connection between its two statements. They generally understand the approaching Hour as the final Resurrection, conceived as an entirely objective, outward event: something that will take place at the end of historical time and bring the entire sequence of worldly events to a close.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01283

But what connection can there be between that final event and the splitting, or breaking open, of the Moon? The Arabic word shaqq suggests both a material object splitting in two and the breaking forth of dawn. If we remain with the outward, literal meaning alone, the problem is made still more difficult by the following verse, which seems to establish the context: “But when they [the unbelievers] see a Sign (âyat), they turn away and say: This is nothing but continuing magic” (54:2).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01284

Literalist commentators have had no difficulty recognizing here an allusion to a miracle performed by the Prophet. According to the story, on a night of the full Moon, one of his relentless opponents from the Quraysh challenged him to produce a Sign proving the prophetic mission he claimed for himself. Those opponents, who denounced the Sign as magic, may actually have had a clearer sense than the devout literalists of the level of reality at which such a Sign can be perceived.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01285

But the central difficulty remains. If the Hour means the final Resurrection, what bearing does a Sign once performed by the Prophet have upon it? How can the splitting of the Moon signify that the Hour is near? If it truly is such a Sign, then the event performed by the Prophet must be understood as a symbolic history, one whose setting is not the world of physical facts and whose meaning is not perceived through the bodily senses. It calls instead for a movement inward: a return (ta’wîl) from the outward event to its hidden, real meaning.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01286

The truth of that meaning becomes apparent when the two parts of the verse acquire the coherence that literalist commentators have been unable to give them. It also means that the Sign of the Hour must be perceived not “on the horizons” (fi’l-âfâq)—not within the objective time of the world, measured by the movements of the stars and extending continuously onward (zamân âfâqî)—but within the soul’s own time. This is inward, subjective, qualitative time, distinguished not by measurable length but by intensity (zamân anfusî).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01287

Literalist interpreters miss the eschatological event when they place it at the end of historical time, as though it were simply the last material occurrence in a series of similar occurrences. The event belongs instead to the soul’s own time. It is the growing intensity of that inward life that brings the event to birth, allowing it to break suddenly into consciousness.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01288

Our philosopher-mystics therefore set aside the questions that modern philology would ordinarily ask about such a verse. Those questions seem to them to pass beside the matter that truly concerns them. They go directly to the issue they consider decisive: we can understand how the Sign appearing in the Moon announces the approaching Hour only by asking in which heaven that Sign occurs and within what kind of time it is true to say that the Hour is near. Their inquiry leads to a remarkable conclusion.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01289

Whatever the moment in historical time, whatever our position beneath the “horizons” of world history, the meaning of the verse depends upon the kind of consciousness for which the Sign actually means something. It depends, therefore, upon the qualitative intensity of the inward time being lived—in other words, upon the depth at which the Sign is spiritually perceived. Sa’inoddin will distinguish seven kinds of spiritual seekers according to the different ways they understand the verse, whether their understanding is illusory or authentic. Each way of understanding reveals, without possibility of self-deception, the person’s inner mode of being. It thereby places that person within a hierarchy of forms of religious consciousness.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01290

The anonymous Sufi’s treatise examined above was intended to illustrate a saying of the Prophet that speaks of seven inner meanings of the Quran. It described seven groups of spiritual seekers, each corresponding to one of those meanings, because the particular meaning accessible to a person reveals and determines that person's mystical rank.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01291

We shall encounter these seven inner meanings again in ’Alâoddawleh Semnânî, though he relates them not to seven classes of people but to the seven subtle organs, or centers of consciousness, within the individual. Sa’inoddin Ispahânî’s treatise offers another variation. The seven forms of consciousness he identifies and describes in connection with a single Quranic verse do not correspond exactly to the seven levels of inner meaning.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01292

The first two, the lowest ranks, belong to interpreters concerned with the outward, literal meaning. The remaining five belong to seekers of the inner meaning, but their grouping differs somewhat from that proposed by the earlier anonymous author. Philosophers are divided into two groups: the Peripatetics and the Ishrâqiyûn, the theosophers of Light (corresponding to the third and fourth groups in the earlier treatise). This gives us another opportunity to recognize Suhrawardî’s influence on the Shiite theosophy of the period.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01293

Here we should recall a view commonly held by the authors we are studying: the relationship of the Ishrâqiyûn to the Peripatetic philosophers is much like that of the Sufis to the theologians of Kalâm, the discipline of rational theology. The Sufis themselves are gathered into a single group; as described here, they are essentially disciples of Ibn ’Arabî.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01294

Finally, since Sa’inoddin is himself a hurufi—that is, a practitioner of the mystical science of letters—and a Shiite, the two highest ranks of his mystical hierarchy are represented by figures corresponding to his own spiritual commitments.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01295

His treatise has two distinct parts, each devoted to one of the two statements in the Quranic verse. For our purposes, it will be more illuminating to consider them together. There is something further. An indispensable supplement to this treatise is found in the Dabestân-e Madhâhib, the Persian encyclopedia of comparative religion that preserves so much otherwise unique information about religious communities and sects in seventeenth-century India.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01296

One chapter reproduces word for word the section of Sa’inoddin’s treatise concerning the Peripatetics and the Ishrâqiyûn. It also contains an essential discussion missing from our manuscript. We may wonder whether that passage was omitted out of caution or whether it represents a personal addition by the author of the Dabestân, though the latter possibility seems unlikely. In any event, there can be little doubt that the author of the Dabestân had Sa’inoddin’s treatise before him.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s2
2. The Jurists and the Traditionists
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01297

Those who adhere to the outward meaning fall into two groups. The first commands little respect from our philosopher-mystic. It consists of the doctors of religious law (foqahâ) and the Traditionists (Mohaddithûn), the specialists in hadîth, who appoint themselves guardians of the literal meaning of every text and every saying attributed to the Prophet. As Sa’inoddin puts it: “These are people who rest the back of their contentment upon the cushion of conformity (taqlîd).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01298

“Having brought all serious inquiry to a halt once and for all, they are perfectly satisfied with themselves.” There is no point in asking them how the splitting or breaking open of the Moon should be understood. In their eyes, to question its literal truth, to doubt that it was a visible, material event, or even to ask how such a thing could have happened is already to surrender to forbidden innovation (bid’a) and commit heresy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01299

As for the approaching Hour, they see no difficulty if it refers to the great final Gathering of everything that has appeared from the beginning to the end of time, when all will be weighed in the Balance and the righteous separated from the condemned. That Gathering necessarily entails the resurrection of material bodies: every particle of every part of the human body, scattered by death, will come to life again at that supreme Hour. One must not ask how this will happen.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01300

One must simply conform, strictly and literally, to the teaching of the prophets. Does the astronomical Sign refer to a miracle performed by the Prophet or to a prodigy at the end of time? Either way, how does it signify the Hour? It is impossible even to put the question to these interpreters. For the question can only be asked by entering a deeper level of meaning, one that transforms the literal facts themselves. And it is precisely that transformation which these literalist scholars reject with stubborn alarm.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s3
3. The Philosophers of Islam
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01301

The second group of those concerned with the outward meaning deserves more consideration. These are the philosophers of Islam (Hokamâ-ye Islâm) and the orthodox scholastic theologians (Motakallimûn). At least they have gone beyond straightforward literalism. They have had the courage to reflect and reason, and have advanced as far as they could along the path of independent inquiry.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01302

Although their fundamental beliefs (i’tiqâd) lead them to the same answers as the first group on the questions that concern us, they do not forbid themselves to ask how things happen. It is true, Sa’inoddin observes, that when they agree to ask the question, they do so with the firm intention of demonstrating that the material event is possible. Their reasoning rests on two premises.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01303
First, they accept the absolute power of the divine Agent, who can freely bring about whatever he wishes, in any manner he chooses.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01304

Second, they reject the celestial physics of the philosophers inspired by the Greeks, who maintain that the heavenly spheres are made of a subtle substance different from earthly matter and therefore cannot be torn or split apart. The Motakallimûn, by contrast, teach that the spheres and heavenly bodies are of the same nature as bodies composed of the earthly elements. They can consequently be torn or divided like anything else accessible to the senses.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01305

From the standpoint of Greek-inspired cosmology, this amounts to an extraordinary physical paradox. It also prevents these theologians from moving beyond the realm of sensible things to an intermediate level of reality. They face a further difficulty in determining the status of a being that is genuinely real while existing outside the divine Being.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01306

Nevertheless, once their premises are granted, it becomes possible to accept that the event in question occurred in the visible, astronomical heavens, as a Sign intended to establish the truth of the prophetic Message before those who denied it.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01307

The same premises help them address the event that announces the approaching Hour. Philosophers object that something which has been completely annihilated cannot return to existence as the numerically identical individual it once was. The resurrection of material bodies as imagined by the Motakallimûn is therefore, they argue, absurd. The theologians reply that it is no more absurd than the original creation of that individual, who was brought into existence when previously he was nothing. Such an argument will convince only those who are already convinced.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01308

Yet in Sa’inoddin’s eyes, this does not deprive the Motakallimûn of their achievement. Given their premises, their conclusions follow necessarily; and at least they have taken the trouble to construct those premises. With a touch of humor, he concludes that they represent a definite kind of consciousness: the person who works hard to extract arguments from the Book and the traditions in order to confirm an interpretation that remains entirely literal. If their powers of philosophical reflection went no further, it was because the wisdom of the Most Wise judged that, for their purposes, they had no need of a capacity exceeding what was required to argue about the letter and its outward meaning.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s4
4. The Peripatetics
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01309

With the third group we enter the company of those who seek the inner meaning. Here we witness the first transformation of the literal facts. From that transformation emerges an esoteric meaning that makes it possible to understand what the splitting of the Moon may signify and how it announces the approaching Hour. Although this group gives us access to the first level of inner meaning, it is still described, in contrast to the Ishrâqiyûn of Suhrawardî’s school, as the group of “outward philosophers” (Hokamâ-ye zâhir). These are the thinkers commonly called Peripatetics (Mashshâ’ûn), whose master was Aristotle and whose leading representative in Islam was Avicenna, known as their chief (ra’îs) and shaykh.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01310

Sa’inoddin tells us that an argument of compelling certainty has led these philosophers to the conviction that the Moon, although it is visible to the senses, cannot possibly be broken or split in any way. According to an axiom of their cosmology, the ethereal matter of the heavens is entirely incapable of undergoing the changes and accidents that affect earthly matter beneath the Moon.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01311
Yet neither reason nor any authority in the world can legitimately compel us to accept an absurdity.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01312

We must therefore acknowledge that the splitting of the Moon mentioned in the Quranic verse has another meaning. It must express a symbol (ramz), pointing toward an event whose true setting is not the visible heaven of astronomy. At the very outset, philosophy thus challenges religious reflection to turn away from the “horizons”—the outer world—and toward the inner world of the soul. The spiritual thinkers we are studying never imagined that a religious person must find either the home or the triumph of faith in absurdity. They accepted the shathîyât, those paradoxical mystical utterances that challenge conventional assumptions, and they sometimes delighted in their almost “divine-human” character.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01313
But they were careful not to confuse what lies beyond ordinary reason with what contradicts reason altogether. To them, absurdity could only be an affront to the divine.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01314

Another fundamental principle opens the way for these philosophers to enter the realm of inner reality—one of the basic ideas (osûl) to which they have devoted their most careful investigations. Every visible star (kawkab) and every heaven (falak) has a corresponding invisible, inward reality (bâtin): an Intelligence that they call the Angel of that star or heaven. Among these Intelligences, the inward reality of the Moon is identified as the “Agent” or “Active Intelligence” (’Aql fa’âl).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01315

The highest degree of human perfection, its final seal, is reached when the spiritual seeker enters into conjunction with this Active Intelligence. The splitting of the Moon in the Quranic verse symbolizes precisely this conjunction with the Intelligence that is the Angel, the hidden reality of the Moon’s heaven. To acquire the stable disposition, or habitus, that makes frequent conjunction with the Active Intelligence possible is to attain the degree called the “acquired intellect,” intellectus adeptus (’aql mostafâd).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01316

Whatever the sage who has reached this degree turns toward, he knows it immediately, without needing to work through a fresh sequence of mental arguments. Since this degree represents the highest limit and final seal of human perfection, the state symbolized by the “splitting of the Moon” must also have belonged to the person who was the Seal of the Prophets.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01317

This interpretation already confirms the theme outlined in the preceding chapter. It reminds us that the intellectus sanctus, the “holy intellect” or highest degree of human intelligence, is a special gift shared by the prophet and the philosophical sage. Because they share that gift, it becomes the source of a prophetic wisdom—a prophetic philosophy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01318

The Angel of Knowledge is none other than the Angel of Revelation. What takes place is not a secularization of prophetic Revelation, but precisely the reverse: philosophical knowledge becomes sacred as it reaches the point where it surpasses its own ordinary limits. The spiritual state of the prophet thus becomes the model for the mystic’s experience, while mystical experience brings philosophy to completion in a metaphysics of ecstasy. It is in this sense that Suhrawardî’s Ishrâq fulfilled Avicenna’s project of an “Eastern wisdom.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01319

The coherence of the Quranic verse now becomes apparent. The splitting of the Moon is a Sign of the Hour—a connection that neither the devout literalists nor the theologians of Kalâm could establish, because they could not penetrate to the depth at which its meaning comes into view. As the author of the Dabestân will emphasize, the splitting of the Moon symbolizes the passage to the inner meaning. For that meaning to unfold, there must be a ta’wîl, a return to the hidden truth.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01320

But this cannot merely be an operation performed upon a text; it must also be an event within the soul. The movement is from the Moon’s outward appearance—the astronomical body visible to everyone—to its inward reality, the Angel of the Moon’s heaven. In Avicennian cosmology, that Angel is the Active Intelligence, the Noûs poêtikos. The passage leads from a sensible reality to its Angel. This is why interpreting the text through ta’wîl cannot succeed unless the soul simultaneously undergoes its own ta’wîl, its own “return” to its source.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01321

And this Return is precisely its resurrection. Resurrection does not mean an event that will take place one day at the far end of the series of events unfolding beneath the “horizons” of natural time. Nor does it mean the resurrection of material bodies, which these philosophers regard as both inconceivable and unnecessary. It means spiritual Resurrection: the soul’s return to its own world.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01322

The orthodox theologians had imagined the final fulfillment of all things taking place within the time measured by the movements of the visible heavens. The philosophers understand the event as something inward. The human being has a twofold task. First, to serve as the mediator through whom things become manifest, since the human being contains a summary of them all—a microcosm.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01323

Second, through acts of knowledge and contemplation, to lead those things back (ta’wîl) from their outward appearance to their inner reality, in a process that is at once an inward turning and an integration. Whenever a human being brings this process to perfection, that person becomes a world in himself (’âlam), an Aeon—what the Latin Avicennians would call a saeculum intelligibile, an intelligible world. He returns to the place of his Return (ma’âd), which is also the place of his origin: the world of pure, immaterial substances, untouched by the perishable matter of the world beneath the Moon. In that world, everything that exists possesses knowledge and perception, and neither ignorance nor anything harmful can exist.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01324

This Return does not occur beneath the “horizons,” as an event belonging to the time of the world (zamân âfâqî), even if it were the final event of that time. It occurs when outward, worldly time—the time associated with literal, outward meaning—is transformed into the soul’s pure inward time (zamân anfusî), the time of inner meaning (see Book I, Chapter IV, §5). This, Sa’inoddin explains, is what is meant when we say that the Prophet “inaugurated the Cycle of the Moon.”
